research_questions: How can prompts describe visible facial movement without exposing numeric FACS codes or assigning an emotion label?
Which regional changes, intensity levels, combinations, and asymmetries remain legible in a single illustration?
How should a still image imply onset, peak, or release while avoiding claims about a subject's inner state?

mechanisms.statement: Represent the face first as observable component motion rather than as a message that proves a named emotion.
Decompose a facial display into independently visible brow, eyelid, cheek, lip, mouth, and jaw changes that can combine without a fixed emotion template.
Specify a low, medium, or high visible displacement for selected regions because spontaneous facial actions vary in graded intensity rather than only presence or absence.
Allow left-right differences only when the prompt names the side and the visible feature change, not a personality or sincerity interpretation.
Compose two or three compatible regional changes and leave their perceived affect open unless the user explicitly requests a displayed reading.
Translate temporal onset, apex, or release into a still-frame cue such as a just-rising brow, held mouth tension, or easing jaw, while treating the phase as an illustration hypothesis.
Convert research codes into ordinary visible phrases and prevent numeric action-unit notation from reaching the generation prompt.
Limit selected motions to those whose displacement and silhouette survive the intended crop and display size.

candidate_definitions.ofm_inner_brow_lift: Describe the inner ends of the eyebrows visibly lifting, with an optional low, medium, or high displacement.
candidate_definitions.ofm_upper_lid_widen: Describe the upper eyelids lifting enough to reveal more of the eyes, without naming a resulting emotion.
candidate_definitions.ofm_lid_cheek_tension: Describe narrowed eyelid openings and visibly raised or tightened cheeks as separate observable changes.
candidate_definitions.ofm_lip_corner_direction: Describe one or both lip corners moving upward, downward, or laterally, including explicit asymmetry when needed.
candidate_definitions.ofm_mouth_opening_shape: Describe the visible mouth aperture as closed, slightly parted, vertically open, or laterally stretched.
candidate_definitions.ofm_jaw_lowering: Describe a visibly lowered jaw and its degree without treating it as proof of surprise, fear, or any other state.
candidate_definitions.ofm_left_right_asymmetry: Assign a named visible facial change to one side while leaving the opposite side neutral or differently displaced.
candidate_definitions.ofm_intensity_combination_router: Choose a small compatible set of regional movements and their visible intensity according to crop, stylization, occlusion, and user constraints.
candidate_definitions.ofm_au_code_prompt_guard: Reject numeric action-unit codes and replace them with plain observable facial phrases before prompt assembly.
candidate_definitions.ofm_inner_state_inference_guard: Prevent facial movement candidates from asserting hidden emotion, sincerity, deception, personality, diagnosis, or intent.
candidate_definitions.ofm_thumbnail_motion_legibility_metric: Measure whether the selected facial changes remain distinguishable at the requested crop and thumbnail size.

pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_inner_brow_lift: The inner brow endpoints are visibly higher than the outer or neutral brow baseline.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_upper_lid_widen: The upper eyelid margin exposes more iris or sclera than the chosen neutral baseline.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_lid_cheek_tension: The eye opening is visibly compressed while the cheek contour rises or tightens beneath it.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_lip_corner_direction: At least one lip corner has a legible upward, downward, or lateral displacement.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_mouth_opening_shape: A readable negative-space shape separates the lips, or the closed-lip contour is explicitly maintained.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_jaw_lowering: The lower jaw and chin sit visibly below the neutral relation to the upper face.
pixel_evidence_definitions.ofm_left_right_asymmetry: The named side differs visibly from the opposite side in one specified facial feature.

compatibility: Regional facial movements combine with gaze direction when eye visibility and eyelid state remain physically compatible.
Low-intensity movement works with close portraits; higher displacement may be required for distant full-body crops.
Facial asymmetry can combine with head rotation if the visible side is stated explicitly.
Observable facial phrases can coexist with displayed-affect hypotheses as long as the latter remain separate and defeasible.
conflicts: Wide exposed eyes conflict with fully closed eyelids in the same instant.
A tightly closed mouth conflicts with a visibly lowered jaw unless a special anatomical or mask design explains it.
Dense hair, masks, hands, or props covering a facial region conflict with requiring pixel evidence from that region.
Numeric FACS notation in the final image prompt conflicts with ordinary visible-language generation.
counterexamples: A helmeted character may communicate through head angle or external display lights while no human facial movement is visible.
A graphic chibi face may use one simple line change rather than anatomically detailed regional motion.
A deliberately neutral or unreadable face can be the requested result and should close all facial-motion slots.
A nonhuman face with movable plates or compound eyes may need species-specific motion primitives instead of human-like brows and lips.
boundaries: Treat facial changes as observable signs, never direct proof of a named inner emotion.
Do not infer sincerity, deception, morality, personality, neurotype, illness, pain, or diagnosis from facial appearance.
Do not expose FACS numbers or research annotation labels as generation tokens.
Respect explicit neutral-expression, mask, no-face, and face-occlusion requests.
domain_limits: The candidates primarily cover visible human or human-like faces in static illustration.
They do not constitute clinical assessment, lie detection, emotion recognition, or biometric identification.
Temporal phase phrases are still-image adaptations and are not validated motion measurements.
embodiment_limits: Facial morphology, disability, paralysis, scarring, age, stylization, and species design can alter or remove expected visible displacements.
Head rotation, foreshortening, makeup, facial hair, masks, and lighting can hide apparent asymmetry or intensity.
Use only regions that the depicted embodiment can visibly articulate.
cultural_limits: No regional movement is encoded as a culturally universal emotion message.
Display conventions and viewer interpretations can vary across communities and situations.
Do not route facial candidates from ethnicity, nationality, or cultural identity.
source_biases: FACS-derived work privileges anatomically described human facial motion and may underrepresent stylized, disabled, or nonhuman embodiments.
DISFA contains 27 young adults recorded under a specific elicitation setup and annotates only a subset of facial actions.
Automated classification evidence does not guarantee faithful synthesis by an image model.
runtime_implications: Store facial motion in a global orthogonal pool rather than a concept-owned route.
Route by visible anatomy, crop, occlusion, intensity, and closed-slot constraints, then select at most a small compatible cluster.
Compile every selected atom into plain visual language and strip annotation codes before prompt emission.
Keep displayed-affect labels in a separate optional layer so facial motion remains reusable.
evaluation_implications: Validate that every selected atom has visible pixel evidence without consulting its intended emotion label.
Check facial candidates at native scale and delivery thumbnail size.
Score anatomical compatibility, side correctness, occlusion, and unintended code leakage separately.
Use diverse human-like and nonhuman holdouts and record abstention when the face cannot support the atom.

title: Classifying Facial Actions
authority: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence article preserved by PubMed Central
limitations: The paper evaluates automatic classification rather than image-generation prompt design.
Its FACS framing is human-anatomy centered and does not validate stylized or nonhuman faces.
Component motion descriptions do not by themselves establish emotion, intent, sincerity, personality, or diagnosis.

title: DISFA: A Spontaneous Facial Action Intensity Database
authority: IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing dataset paper hosted by the dataset creator
limitations: DISFA includes 27 young adults, approximately 130000 frames, and twelve annotated facial actions in a controlled video-elicitation setting.
The sample and recording conditions do not establish population-wide or cross-cultural representativeness.
Framewise action intensity is evidence about observed motion, not ground truth for hidden emotion or a guarantee of still-image legibility.

research_questions: How can a prompt distinguish what a character visibly displays from what a viewer may perceive and from any unknowable inner state?
Which face, body, surrounding-person, and interaction cues support congruent, mixed, or ambiguous readings?
How can runtime selection avoid universalizing one group's context weighting or turning affect cues into personality and diagnosis claims?

mechanisms.statement: Treat a face as one visible cue among several and never as ground truth for the depicted person's internal emotion.
Compose face and body evidence explicitly because body context can materially change the valence viewers assign to an intense face.
Represent surrounding people's visible displays and spatial relationship because social context can alter the perceived affect of a focal figure.
Preserve alternative readings because observers from different sampled cultural contexts may allocate attention differently between focal and surrounding people.
Use aligned or conflicting face, body, and social cues as a visible design relation rather than resolving every scene to one emotion label.
Store observable display atoms separately from an optional perceived-affect hypothesis and never convert that hypothesis into an inner-state assertion.
When cues conflict, retain one legible tension and avoid adding enough labels or symbols to force a single interpretation.
Evaluate whether viewers report a bounded distribution of readings instead of scoring one intended label as the sole correct answer.

candidate_definitions.dpa_face_body_cue_alignment: Align a visible facial movement cluster with posture, muscle tension, and action energy that point toward a similar displayed reading.
candidate_definitions.dpa_face_body_cue_tension: Place a visible facial movement cluster in tension with body posture or action energy, leaving the mismatch perceptible rather than explaining it as hidden truth.
candidate_definitions.dpa_foreground_background_affect_contras: Contrast the focal figure's visible display with clearly different expressions or postures in surrounding figures.
candidate_definitions.dpa_social_response_context: Show another person's observable response, orientation, and distance as context for how the focal display may be read.
candidate_definitions.dpa_visible_restraint_pattern: Use a small, contained cluster such as compressed lips, limited movement, and held posture, described only as visible restraint.
candidate_definitions.dpa_mixed_display_cue_cluster: Combine two visibly different cue families without collapsing them into a single named emotion.
candidate_definitions.dpa_perceived_affect_hypothesis_router: Optionally select a tentative displayed or viewer-perceived affect description from the full visible cue configuration, marked as a hypothesis.
candidate_definitions.dpa_inner_state_nonclaim_guard: Block claims that the visible display proves what the character truly feels, wants, remembers, or intends.
candidate_definitions.dpa_cultural_universality_guard: Block claims that one cue weighting or affect reading is universal across cultures and viewers.
candidate_definitions.dpa_personality_diagnosis_guard: Block personality, morality, neurotype, deception, pathology, and diagnosis conclusions from affect cues.
candidate_definitions.dpa_reading_distribution_metric: Collect multiple plausible viewer readings and measure cue visibility and ambiguity without requiring one emotion label.

pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_face_body_cue_alignment: The face, torso, limbs, and action energy contain at least two mutually compatible visible cue families.
pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_face_body_cue_tension: At least one facial cue and one bodily or action cue visibly point toward different plausible readings.
pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_foreground_background_affect_contras: The focal and surrounding figures show distinguishable facial or postural cue configurations.
pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_social_response_context: A second figure has a visible orientation, distance, and response directed toward the focal figure or shared event.
pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_visible_restraint_pattern: Several low-amplitude cues are visibly contained without an accompanying claim about concealed feeling.
pixel_evidence_definitions.dpa_mixed_display_cue_cluster: Two contrasting observable cue families remain simultaneously legible at the delivery scale.

compatibility: Displayed-affect atoms combine with observable facial motion when the exact facial changes remain independently specified.
Face-body alignment can combine with clear action phases and prop interaction.
Face-body tension is compatible with authorial ambiguity when only one major contradiction is foregrounded.
Social response context combines with gaze topology and proxemics when all targets remain spatially legible.
conflicts: An inner-emotion declaration conflicts with a displayed or perceived affect hypothesis.
A universal emotion lookup from one facial feature conflicts with contextual and cultural variation.
A subtle mixed display conflicts with a distant crop that erases its component cues.
Multiple contradictory cue clusters of equal salience conflict with a bounded ambiguity budget.
counterexamples: A broad smile on a face attached to an exhausted collapsing body may not be perceived as simple happiness.
The same central cartoon face can be judged differently when surrounding characters display congruent versus incongruent expressions.
A masked character can create a strong perceived affect through posture and social reaction without visible facial evidence.
A deliberately iconic emoji-like image may intentionally request one conventional label and close contextual ambiguity.
boundaries: Use displayed and perceived language; never assert emotional ground truth from pixels.
Do not infer personality, morality, deception, trauma, neurotype, illness, or diagnosis.
Do not turn findings from Japanese and Western samples into national or ethnic character rules.
Preserve user requests for neutral, unreadable, masked, or deliberately ambiguous affect.
domain_limits: The sources study human observers and mostly human or cartoon human figures, not all stylized, creature, or machine embodiments.
High-intensity findings do not automatically transfer to ordinary low-intensity scenes.
Perceived-affect design does not measure commercial appeal, empathy, or long-term attachment.
embodiment_limits: Bodies, faces, ears, tails, wings, screens, and other expressive channels differ in visibility and articulation.
Disability, masking, restraint, armor, and species design may make a conventional cue unavailable.
Do not penalize low facial mobility when other visible channels carry the scene.
cultural_limits: Culture can influence attention allocation and interpretation, but the cited samples do not define homogeneous East and West populations.
Affect terms, display rules, genre conventions, and surrounding-person cues can be learned differently.
Runtime selection must not use ethnicity or nationality as a deterministic affect router.
source_biases: The intense-emotion study focuses on peak positive and negative situations and cannot define everyday displays.
The cultural-context study compares bounded Japanese and Western samples using specific cartoon and eye-tracking tasks.
Both sources concern human judgments and do not directly validate text-to-image model behavior.
runtime_implications: Keep observable face, body, and social-context candidates in separate orthogonal pools, then assemble a small visible relation bundle.
Treat perceived affect as an optional downstream hypothesis, never as the source of hidden-state facts.
Allow aligned, mixed, or unresolved modes; creativity may widen cue distance but must preserve pixel-legible context.
Close affect slots when the user requests neutrality, opacity, or no emotional direction.
evaluation_implications: Blind reviewers should describe visible cues before offering any affect reading.
Record the distribution and confidence of plausible readings instead of only exact-label accuracy.
Test face-only, body-only, full-context, and context-swapped variants to detect overreliance on one channel.
Include culturally diverse reviewers only as scoped evidence and never use disagreement to stereotype groups.

title: Body Cues, Not Facial Expressions, Discriminate Between Intense Positive and Negative Emotions
authority: Science article PDF hosted by the first author's academic laboratory
limitations: The experiments concern intense positive and negative real-life expressions and composites, not the full range of everyday affect.
Viewer judgments of valence do not establish the depicted person's inner state.
The study does not validate stylized illustration prompts, nonhuman embodiments, or universal cross-cultural interpretation.

title: Placing the Face in Context: Cultural Differences in the Perception of Facial Emotion
authority: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology article PDF hosted by the first author's university laboratory
limitations: The two studies use bounded Japanese and Western participant samples and specific cartoon displays, so results must not be essentialized to whole cultures.
The work examines perception and attention, not emotional truth, personality, or diagnosis.
Its task design does not directly establish how generated subculture illustrations will be interpreted across formats and audiences.

research_questions: How can eye direction, head orientation, scene geometry, and visible targets form a reusable attention topology?
How should mutual gaze, joint attention, split attention, and off-frame attention be distinguished in a single image?
Which guards prevent head direction from being treated as exact gaze or gaze from being treated as proof of intention?

mechanisms.statement: Combine the visible head region with scene layout rather than estimating an attention target from isolated eyes alone.
Represent eye direction and head orientation as separate cues that may align, diverge, or become unavailable under occlusion.
Give an in-frame gaze vector a named, visible target whose location plausibly intersects the depicted eye and head geometry.
Mark attention as explicitly off-frame when the vector exits the composition instead of inventing an unseen in-frame target.
Encode joint attention as two or more people visibly converging on one common target, with each person and target spatially separable.
Treat two people looking at each other as mutual gaze, distinct from joint attention toward a third target.
Lower confidence or abstain when eyelids, pupils, head rotation, distance, or occlusion make the target unreadable.
Use gaze as visible attention evidence while blocking claims that it proves thought, desire, deception, or future action.

candidate_definitions.gha_eye_head_same_target: Align visible eye direction and head orientation toward the same named person, object, event, or camera target.
candidate_definitions.gha_eye_head_split_target: Turn the head toward one direction while the visible eyes redirect toward another named target.
candidate_definitions.gha_visible_target_line: Place a visible in-frame target along a plausible line from the eyes or face orientation through scene depth.
candidate_definitions.gha_joint_attention_convergence: Direct two or more figures toward one common visible target while keeping each gaze source and the target separable.
candidate_definitions.gha_mutual_gaze_pair: Direct two figures toward each other's visible face or eye region without introducing a third shared target.
candidate_definitions.gha_off_frame_attention_exit: Aim the visible attention vector through a named frame edge and leave its target outside the composition.
candidate_definitions.gha_attention_topology_router: Choose direct-to-camera, single-target, split, mutual, joint, or off-frame topology from cast size, target availability, anatomy, and user constraints.
candidate_definitions.gha_occlusion_anatomy_guard: Reject or weaken gaze atoms when eyes, pupils, face orientation, or species-specific attention organs cannot visibly support them.
candidate_definitions.gha_head_only_gaze_guard: Prevent head direction alone from being described as precise eye gaze when the eyes are unavailable.
candidate_definitions.gha_intention_nonclaim_guard: Prevent attention topology from asserting thought, desire, deception, agreement, hostility, or predicted action.
candidate_definitions.gha_target_intersection_metric: Measure whether each selected attention vector reaches its declared target or frame exit at delivery scale.

pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_eye_head_same_target: The pupils or eye openings and head orientation visibly converge on the same declared target region.
pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_eye_head_split_target: The visible eyes deviate from the face orientation toward a second declared target without impossible anatomy.
pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_visible_target_line: A plausible ray from the depicted attention organ or face intersects a visible target rather than empty unrelated space.
pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_joint_attention_convergence: At least two distinct gaze or head vectors converge on one visible target region.
pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_mutual_gaze_pair: Each of two figures' visible attention vectors terminates on the other figure's face or eye region.
pixel_evidence_definitions.gha_off_frame_attention_exit: The attention vector clearly leaves through the declared edge without intersecting a competing in-frame target.

compatibility: Eye-head alignment combines with direct portrait address and a clear camera target.
Split eye-head direction combines with cautious checking or divided attention only when both directions remain readable.
Joint attention combines with shared prop interaction and group staging.
Off-frame attention combines with negative space and anticipated action beyond the crop.
conflicts: Closed or fully occluded eyes conflict with a precise pupil-based gaze claim.
Two figures looking at each other conflict with labeling the configuration as joint attention toward a third target.
A declared target outside the plausible eye-head ray conflicts with target intersection.
Several equal candidate targets near one ray conflict with a claim of unambiguous attention.
counterexamples: A back-facing head may suggest broad orientation but cannot support precise pupil direction.
A cyclopean creature can support one gaze ray but should not inherit two-eye convergence assumptions.
A blindfolded character can face an object without providing visible eye-gaze evidence.
A poster may deliberately direct every character to separate off-frame targets to produce fragmentation rather than joint attention.
boundaries: Gaze is visible attention evidence, not proof of thoughts, motives, consent, deception, or future behavior.
Head orientation alone must not be mislabeled as exact gaze.
Do not infer relational valence, personality, diagnosis, or culture from mutual or averted gaze.
Respect explicit eyes-closed, blindfolded, no-eye, no-people, and off-frame-target constraints.
domain_limits: The sources concern human gaze in natural images and static-image target estimation; transfer to stylized and nonhuman illustration requires validation.
Gaze target benchmarks measure localization, not narrative correctness or viewer interpretation.
The candidate set does not model reading order of the external viewer's own eyes.
embodiment_limits: Nonhuman characters may attend through compound eyes, antennae, sensors, head plates, or body orientation rather than human pupils.
Strabismus, monocular vision, blindness, prosthetics, helmets, and stylization alter available cues and must not be treated as errors by default.
Foreshortening, hair, glare, distance, and profile views can make eye direction indeterminate.
cultural_limits: Eye contact and gaze aversion have context-dependent social meanings and must not receive universal moral or emotional labels.
Do not route attention behavior from ethnicity, nationality, gender, age, or cultural identity.
Joint attention is encoded geometrically here, not as a universal claim about social agreement.
source_biases: GazeFollow is a computer-vision benchmark whose labels and image distribution may not cover all illustration styles or embodiments.
The joint-attention study uses a computational extraction method and a bounded human captioning study.
Both sources can encourage overconfidence in gaze localization if uncertainty, occlusion, and multiple targets are ignored.
runtime_implications: Store attention candidates in a global topology pool independent of character concept routes.
Select topology only after cast count, target slots, anatomy, crop, and occlusion are known.
Require every in-frame vector to name a target and every off-frame vector to name an exit edge.
Emit uncertainty or abstain rather than fabricating precise gaze from a hidden face.
evaluation_implications: Trace each selected vector on the rendered image and verify target intersection at native and thumbnail scale.
Score eye direction, head direction, target identity, off-frame state, and occlusion separately.
Test direct gaze, split gaze, mutual gaze, joint attention, distractor targets, profiles, and nonhuman holdouts.
Have blind reviewers describe who appears to look where before asking any question about inferred intention.

title: Where Are They Looking?
authority: MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory project page for the GazeFollow paper and dataset
limitations: The project predicts likely gaze targets from natural images and remains below human performance; it does not provide mind reading or intention ground truth.
Dataset and model evidence may not generalize to stylized, nonhuman, heavily occluded, or extreme-profile illustrations.
The official project summary emphasizes in-image objects, so off-frame routing is a design extension that requires separate validation.

title: Discovery and Usage of Joint Attention in Images
authority: MIT Center for Brains, Minds and Machines publication record for the original study
limitations: The extraction method estimates three-dimensional gaze and depth from a single image and can be wrong under occlusion or ambiguous geometry.
The human study tests sensitivity to simplified joint-attention captions and does not prove intentions or social agreement.
The work does not validate every cast size, culture, stylization, nonhuman embodiment, or image-generation model.
